messages.author: 40bef15e0492270c
messages.subject: Poisson log-linear model
parts:
Hi,

I am trying to fit a poisson log-linear model with multiple groups to some count data. The model can be seen at https://gist.github.com/demodw/982bc7188f1ea906d2085699b4758e57. I have forced the first age-bin to be the reference, by setting it to 0. 

I've tried both using both NUTS-HMC and ADVI, but they are both having trouble. The beta_0 values are is way off, compared to just a single group at a time using rstanarm. Oddly enough, the coefficients beta_A, beta_B, and beta_AB is in the same interval as the model fit from rstanarm. This leads me to believe that there is something wrong with the mode I have specified. 

Can anyone offer some insight as to what is wrong? Is the model unidentified? Did i miss something important?

Cheers.

ninja-edit: clarification

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson log-linear model
parts:
I don't see anything wrong with the model. You could
make it more efficient computationally, but that's another matter.
With half-normal priors, you're allowing the standard deviations
have support at 0 and it may be that the model is just driving
the result toward complete pooling.

Have you tried simulating data from the model with non-zero standard
deviation parameters to see if that will fit?

You may want to try the non-centered parameterization (use normal(0, 1)
and then multiply by standard deviation) --- that can be much more efficient
with small group counts.

- Bob

P.S. Rather than

beta_AB ~ normal(0, beta_AB_hyper);

we'd write

beta_AB ~ normal(0, sigma_beta_AB);

The "sigma" helps indicate it's a scale (though I
see you don't have means here, which is good given you
have an overall intercept).

messages.author: 40bef15e0492270c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson log-linear model
parts:
I should have looked in the manual, I guess. :-)


I did a bit more of searching, and read that the negative binomial distribution can also handle zero cases like this, so I decided to try it out before moving to the (in my eyes) more advanced (and maybe not so easy to interpret) zero-inflated model. 


The model was straight forward to implement, and required only very few modifications to the original code (Go Stan!). I uploaded the model here: https://gist.github.com/demodw/457aaff455b99bd5a36fa8961fb3c8bb. I just put normal(0,5) on the intercept, and normal(0, 2.5) on the coefficients.  When I run the model without any priors on sigma for each regression coefficient, the model converges nicely (R-hat < 1, tree depth ~ 8.5, log-posterior looks unimodal). Step-size is about 0.01 in all chains, so quite low, which may be due to the relatively weak priors (I guess). The coefficients are approximately the same as  if I had run it in 4 separate rstanarm runs. So far so good. 


However, when I try to add priors on the scale values, I run into trouble. I uploaded the model to https://gist.github.com/demodw/37a7bb1a8e4cb6769f3ee1cf45ad2a25. The intercept is modelled with a normal(0, 2.5) prior on the scale, and the coefficients are modelled with a normal(0, 1) prior on the scale. I would have thought this corresponded approximately to the scenario above, since normal(0, 2.5) has support for values in the range +-5.7, and normal(0, 1) has support for the values in the range +-2.2. The model does converge (R-hat < 1.1, tree-depth ~6.5). Step-size is is about four times at large, at 0.04, in all chains. However there are quite a few divergences. From the inspection of energy and log-posterior, it also seems that it is now multi-model (see attachments). Initially I thought that the model might be unidentified, but I cannot really see why. I have coded male/female as -1, 1. The other categorical variable, Adm, I have forced to have a zero entry. 


When I inspect each of the coefficients, they all look to behave nicely. They are within the bounds, and look normally distributed. Similar with the scale values, except I start seeing some tails, especially on sigma_A and sigma_B. For these two it seems that Stan tried to explored beyond the bounds of the specified distribution. So, naturally, I tried to increase these a bit. The result was the same: lots of divergences, and Stan once again tried to explore beyond the bonds. I've tried with both double exponential, cauchy, and student_t with 3 and 7 df. Same result. Even increasing the acceptance rate to 0.95 did not change it. Am I missing something? Is there an unidentified component in my model?


Cheers,

David

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Poisson log-linear model
parts:
> On Nov 30, 2016, at 7:03 PM, David Westergaard <da...@harsk.dk> wrote:
>
> Hi,
>
> Some more fiddling around and I seem to have working model now. hurray. Now I'm just wondering if it can be made computationally better. Right now I am just looping over each data point.
>
> Any advice?

It might be better statistically moving to the non-centered
parameterization (it's location and log scale that get "non-centered").

You can rewrite your loop

for (n in 1:N) {
real eta;
eta = beta0[Di[n]] +
betaSex[Di[n]]*Sex[n] +
betaAge[Di[n]]*age_z[n] +
betaAdm2[Di[n]]*Adm2[n] +
betaAdm3[Di[n]]*Adm3[n] +
betaA[Di[n]]*A[n] +
betaB[Di[n]]*B[n] +
betaAB[Di[n]]*AB[n] +
logOffset[n];
// Increment likelihood
target += neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(Count[n] | eta, phi[Di[n]] );
}

as

vector[N] eta;
eta = beta0[Di]
+ betaSex[Di] .* Sex
...
+ logOffset;
Count ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta, phi[Di]);

as long as all those variables are vectors.

- Bob

Den onsdag den 30. november 2016 kl. 18.23.02 UTC-8 skrev Bob Carpenter:

It might be better statistically moving to the non-centered
parameterization (it's location and log scale that get "non-centered").

Fit didn't really seem to improve, and tree depth increased from 6 to 8, so computation time also went quite a bit up. Truth be told I've never really had luck with the Matt trick for multilevel models. I attached the modified script for those interested.

You can rewrite your loop

    for (n in 1:N) {
      real eta;
      eta = beta0[Di[n]] +
        betaSex[Di[n]]*Sex[n] +
        betaAge[Di[n]]*age_z[n] +
        betaAdm2[Di[n]]*Adm2[n] +
        betaAdm3[Di[n]]*Adm3[n] +
        betaA[Di[n]]*A[n] +
        betaB[Di[n]]*B[n] +
        betaAB[Di[n]]*AB[n] +
        logOffset[n];
      // Increment likelihood
      target += neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(Count[n] | eta, phi[Di[n]] );
    }

as

 vector[N] eta;
 eta = beta0[Di]
       + betaSex[Di] .* Sex
       ...
       + logOffset;
 Count ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta, phi[Di]);

as long as all those variables are vectors.

Is that actually faster, computationally, or does it just look cleaner?

Thanks.

David

> eta = beta0[Di[n]] +
> betaSex[Di[n]]*Sex[n] +
> betaAge[Di[n]]*age_z[n] +
> betaAdm2[Di[n]]*Adm2[n] +
> betaAdm3[Di[n]]*Adm3[n] +
> betaA[Di[n]]*A[n] +
> betaB[Di[n]]*B[n] +
> betaAB[Di[n]]*AB[n] +
> logOffset[n];
> // Increment likelihood
> target += neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(Count[n] | eta, phi[Di[n]] );
> }
>
> as
>
> vector[N] eta;
> eta = beta0[Di]
> + betaSex[Di] .* Sex
> ...
> + logOffset;
> Count ~ neg_binomial_2_log(eta, phi[Di]);
>
> as long as all those variables are vectors.
>
>
> Is that actually faster, computationally, or does it just look cleaner?

It'll be faster for two reasons. First, the scalar vector
products can produce much more compact pieces of the overall
expression graph. Second, vectorizing the call to neg_binomial_2
will convert a bunch of virtual functions into a single virtual
function call. How much of a difference it'll make will depend
on the size of N.

Also, Stan doesn't have the same problem as BUGS or R in its
parser, so you can put the operators like "+" on the next line
like you'd see it in other programming languages and in math
typesetting.

- Bob

Fit didn't really seem to improve, and tree depth increased from 6 to 8, so computation time also went quite a bit up. Truth be told I've never really had luck with the Matt trick for multilevel models.

If you have a lot of data, the centered parameterization will
mix better.   We usually see the tree depth going down and

and how much the scale component.
Yea that could be it. For some groups I only have small counts, but for most groups the counts are quite high.

I attached the modified script for those interested. 



You can rewrite your loop 

   for (n in 1:N) { 
     real eta; 
     eta = beta0[Di[n]] + 
       betaSex[Di[n]]*Sex[n] + 
       betaAge[Di[n]]*age_z[n] + 
       betaAdm2[Di[n]]*Adm2[n] + 
       betaAdm3[Di[n]]*Adm3[n] + 
       betaA[Di[n]]*A[n] + 
       betaB[Di[n]]*B[n] + 
       betaAB[Di[n]]*AB[n] + 
       logOffset[n]; 
     // Increment likelihood 
     target += neg_binomial_2_log_lpmf(Count[n] | eta, phi[Di[n]] );

We don't actually know what's hard for our black-box
variational inference. We do know it's best if the unconstrained
posterior is roughly multivariate normal.

The whole thing's a great research problem, because as
far as I can tell, most of the computer scientists using
VB aren't trying to calibrate it w.r.t. the full Bayesian
solution. The only work I know along these lines (and I'd
hope there'd be more somewhere) is by Matt Wand at UTS
in Sydney.

- Bob
